505.title: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)
505.hook: even in war, fruit trees are spared; the rabbis made it a ban on all waste
505.howItsDone: Bal tashchit is a recognized principle of Jewish law, applied to waste of food, objects, energy and resources, and Jewish environmental teaching often begins from this verse about the fruit trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king who writes out the law and reads it every day. Your line was even the king reads. What line did you read before using your power? Today, a law for the middle of a war. Day five hundred five.

A city won't open its gates. The army camped outside has axes, and all around the walls stand orchards. Olive trees, fig trees, date palms that took years to grow. Cut them down, and you get timber for siege works, and you break the people inside: hungry now, and poorer for years after. In war, the usual limits tend to fall away. And right in the middle of the Torah's laws of war, there's a verse that stops an army at the edge of an orchard.
screen: `A CITY WON'T OPEN ITS GATES.` → `ORCHARDS AROUND THE WALLS.` →`AN ARMY STOPS AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish translation: when you besiege a city a long time, "thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by wielding an axe against them." You may eat from them. You may not cut them down. And then a question: "for is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged of thee?" The tree isn't your enemy. It can't run behind the walls. Why make it a casualty? The Hebrew can also be read as a statement: for man is a tree of the field. The medieval commentator Ibn Ezra reads it that way: people live from trees, so destroying them destroys your own life. Two readings, one point. From the words thou shalt not destroy, lo tashchit, the rabbis built a whole principle, called bal tashchit: do not destroy needlessly. And they took it far beyond orchards and far beyond war. Maimonides writes that anyone who smashes dishes, tears clothes, wrecks a building, blocks a spring or wastes food destructively breaks this law. In the Talmud, one rabbi goes further still: someone who could eat barley bread but eats the costlier wheat bread has broken it. Others there push back that caring for your own body comes first, but the reach of the idea is clear. The logic runs like this. If even in war, when everything feels permitted, you can't destroy a tree for no reason, then in peacetime, in your own kitchen, how much more. Waste isn't only careless. In this tradition, it's a kind of small destruction.
screen: `DON'T TAKE THE AXE TO THE TREES.` · `IS THE TREE A MAN?` · `BAL TASHCHIT: DON'T DESTROY.` · `IF IN WAR, HOW MUCH MORE IN PEACE.` · then, large: `DON'T DESTROY NEEDLESSLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: waste nothing today. Settle, and breathe. Picture your day in things. The food in your fridge that's close to turning. The lights left on in empty rooms. The shirt you'll throw out over one loose button. The water running while you brush your teeth. Pick three. For each, picture the small act that saves it instead. Eating the leftovers. Flipping the switch. Sewing the button. Notice that each one is tiny, and each one is a tree left standing. The bell holds the time.
Bal tashchit. Do not destroy. The rabbis' rule against needless destruction and waste, drawn from the fruit trees of Shoftim.
Your line: don't destroy needlessly. Today, save one thing you'd usually throw away: food, water, power, or something that only needs mending. Day five hundred five.

506.title: Shoftim: the nearest town (Deuteronomy 21:1–9)
506.hook: for an unsolved death, the nearest town's elders declare their hands did not shed this blood
506.howItsDone: The heifer rite hasn't been performed for many centuries, but Jewish law still teaches levayah, accompanying a departing guest some distance, which the rabbis drew from the elders' declaration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fruit trees spared even in war, and bal tashchit. Your line was don't destroy needlessly. What did you save? Today, the last scene in Shoftim, and a ritual for a crime nobody solved. Day five hundred six.

A body is found in an open field, between towns. Nobody saw what happened. There's no suspect, no witness, no trail. A case like that can quietly go cold. A file in a drawer. A name nobody says again. The Torah won't let it go cold. It sends out the elders and judges with measuring lines, to find out one thing: which town is closest to where the body lies. And then that town, which did nothing wrong as far as anyone knows, has to answer.
screen: `A BODY IN AN OPEN FIELD.` → `NO WITNESS, NO SUSPECT.` → `MEASURE TO THE NEAREST TOWN.`

segments.voice: The ritual is ancient and stark. The elders of the nearest town take a young heifer that has never worked, down to a valley with flowing water, and the rite is performed there. Then the elders wash their hands over it and say, in the old Jewish translation: "Our hands have not shed this blood, neither have our eyes seen it." It's called the eglah arufah, the heifer whose neck is broken, and the rabbis stopped at the elders' words. The Mishnah, in tractate Sotah, asks: would it ever cross anyone's mind that the elders of the court are murderers? Of course not. So what are they really saying? The Mishnah's answer: he didn't come to us and we send him away without food. We didn't see him and let him go on alone, without someone to walk with him. In other words, the elders are declaring that their town didn't fail him in the small ways. No one turned him away hungry. No one let a stranger walk out onto a dangerous road unescorted. From this the rabbis drew a duty called levayah, accompanying a guest part of the way when they leave. So the strange ritual makes an ordinary point. A death on the road isn't only the killer's business. It's a question for the nearest town: did we feed him? Did we walk with him? The nearest town answers, even when it's innocent.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take some responsibility for your neighborhood. Settle, and breathe. Picture the few blocks around where you live. The corner that's badly lit. The neighbor who hasn't been seen in a while. The person who sleeps in the doorway by the store. The kid who walks home alone. You didn't cause any of it. But you're the nearest town. Pick one, and ask the Mishnah's two questions: is anyone going hungry here, and is anyone walking alone? Decide one small thing you could do. The bell holds the time.
Shoftim. Judges. The portion that ends with elders measuring to the nearest town, and that town answering.
Your line: the nearest town answers. Today, walk a guest out to the door or the car, or check on one neighbor. Day five hundred six.

507.title: Ki Teitzei: the mother bird (Deuteronomy 22:6–7)
507.hook: send the mother bird away before taking the eggs, a command that promises long life
507.howItsDone: Shiluach haken, sending away the mother bird, is still practiced by some Jews, who seek out a nest of a kosher wild bird to fulfill it, and the debate over its reason is a classic of Jewish thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elders of the nearest town: did we feed him, did we walk with him? Your line was the nearest town answers. Who did you check on? Today a new portion, and a nest by the road. Day five hundred seven.

The new portion is Ki Teitzei, when you go out, and it's packed. The medieval Sefer HaChinuch counts seventy-four commandments in it, more than in any other portion. Marriage, debts, lost property, fences, wages, animals. And tucked among them is a scene so small it's easy to miss. You're walking along a road, and there's a bird's nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting on the eggs or the chicks. It's the kind of moment that lasts a few seconds. The Torah stops for it.
screen: `KI TEITZEI: WHEN YOU GO OUT.` → `SEVENTY-FOUR COMMANDMENTS.` → `A NEST BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The law: don't take the mother along with the young. Send the mother away first, and then you may take the eggs or the chicks. And the reward, in the old Jewish translation: "that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days." The Ten Commandments attach the same promise to honoring your father and mother. A weighty family duty and a bird's nest by the road, both rewarded with long days. Why this law? Here the tradition doesn't speak with one voice, and it's worth hearing both. Maimonides, in his Guide for the Perplexed, says it's about compassion: animals feel grief, a mother bird's distress at seeing her young taken is real, and the Torah wants to spare her. Nachmanides says it's about us: the law trains people not to become cruel. But the Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, has a surprise. If a prayer leader says to God, your mercy reaches even to the bird's nest, they silence him. The Talmud explains: he turns God's commandments into mercy, when they are decrees. In this reading, no one should claim to know exactly why God commanded it. It's kept because it's commanded. So one camp says the reason is compassion, another says don't presume a reason at all. Both camps send the mother away. And maybe that's the point of a tiny law with an enormous reward: the smallest act of care counts.
screen: `SEND THE MOTHER AWAY FIRST.` · `THE SAME REWARD AS HONORING PARENTS.` · `COMPASSION, SAYS MAIMONIDES.` · `A DECREE, SAYS THE MISHNAH.` · then, large: `SPARE THE MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with one creature. Settle, and breathe. Think of the creatures you'll cross paths with today. A pet who wants attention. A spider in the bathtub. Birds at a feeder. A neighbor's dog that barks. Even the ant on the counter. Picture one of them, and picture a gentler way of meeting it than usual. Carrying the spider outside. Ten slow minutes with the dog. Water left out. Small. That's the scale of this law. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. A portion crowded with commandments, and a nest by the road.
Your line: spare the mother. Today, be gentle with one creature in a way you'd usually not bother with. Day five hundred seven.

508.title: Ki Teitzei: build the railing (Deuteronomy 22:8)
508.hook: a new house needs a parapet so no one falls
508.howItsDone: Jewish law treats the railing as a real obligation: observant Jews put a parapet around a flat roof or balcony that people use, some say a blessing when building one, and the commandment is cited for home and workplace safety more broadly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother bird sent away, and the debate about why. Your line was spare the mother. Which creature did you treat gently? Today, from a nest to a rooftop. Day five hundred eight.

Houses in ancient Israel had flat roofs, and people used them. They dried flax up there, slept there on hot nights, ate there, talked there. In the Bible, Rahab hides the spies under flax on her roof. A roof was a room without walls. Which meant that on any warm evening, someone, a child chasing a ball, a guest who'd had a little wine, an old man stepping back to see the stars, was one step from a fall. One sentence in Ki Teitzei is about that step.
screen: `FLAT ROOFS, USED LIKE ROOMS.` → `RAHAB'S FLAX.` → `ONE STEP FROM A FALL.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a parapet for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thy house, if any man fall from thence." The Hebrew for parapet is ma'akeh: a low wall, a railing. Notice what it asks. Not that you push no one off the roof. Of course not. It asks you to think ahead about a fall that hasn't happened, to someone you may not even know yet. And if you don't, and someone falls, the verse says the blood is on your house. Not on fate. On you, the builder who could have seen it coming. The rabbis took the railing and ran with it. The Talmud, in Bava Kamma, says a person shouldn't keep a dangerous dog in the house, or leave a rickety ladder standing, because of this verse. Maimonides writes that anything on your property that puts life in danger, an open pit, an uncovered well, a weak wall, has to be fixed, and this is both a positive command and a prohibition. The roof became a stand-in for every hazard you own. Plenty of laws deal with harm after it's done. This one makes prevention the commandment. It says caring for other people includes the dull work of thinking about what could go wrong in your own space, and fixing it before anyone gets hurt.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fix one hazard at home. Settle, and breathe. Walk through your home in your mind, room by room, the way a visitor might. The rug that slides. The stairs with no light. The cord across the floor. The medicine within a small child's reach. The smoke alarm with a dead battery. The pool gate, the loose step, the balcony. Go slowly. Find the one most likely to hurt someone. Picture fixing it, and decide when. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion where a new house needs a railing before anyone falls.
Your line: build the railing. Today, fix the hazard you found, or at least start: a battery, a light, a latch. Day five hundred eight.

509.title: Ki Teitzei: pay today (Deuteronomy 24:14–15)
509.hook: don't hold a poor worker's wages overnight
509.howItsDone: Jewish law forbids delaying payment to workers past the agreed time, called bal talin, and observant employers, from families paying a babysitter to businesses, are taught to pay day workers by the end of the day or night they worked.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the railing around the roof, built before anyone falls. Your line was build the railing. Did you fix your hazard? Today, a law about the end of a work day. Day five hundred nine.

For a lot of people, payday decides what's for dinner. A delivery driver waiting on a platform to release last week's earnings. A freelancer chasing an invoice that's sixty days late. A day laborer outside a hardware store at six in the morning, hoping the cash comes at the end of the shift and not next Friday. For the person paying, a delay is a line on a to-do list. For the person waiting, it's groceries, or not. The Torah draws the line at sunset.
screen: `PAYDAY DECIDES DINNER.` → `AN INVOICE SIXTY DAYS LATE.` → `THE LINE AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: First, the Torah says, don't oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether they're one of your own people or a stranger living in your towns. Then the rule, in the old Jewish translation: "In the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it." Leviticus says it too, from the other side of the clock: don't keep a worker's wages with you overnight until morning. The rabbis called this prohibition bal talin, do not hold it overnight. Now look at the reason. For he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it. In Hebrew, the phrase is closer to: he lifts up his soul to it. His whole self is hanging on that pay. The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, reads those words and asks: why did this worker climb the high ramp, hang from the tree, risk his life? For his wages. So when you hold back what he earned, the Talmud says, it's as if you've taken his life. That's strong language for a late payment. But it's the worker's view, not the employer's. The one who pays sees an amount. The one who's paid sees a day of his life, already spent, waiting to come back as bread. The verse ends with a warning: or he will cry to the LORD against you, and it will be counted as sin. The cry of the unpaid is heard.
screen: `DON'T OPPRESS THE POOR WORKER.` · `BEFORE THE SUN GOES DOWN.` · `HE LIFTS UP HIS SOUL TO IT.` · `HE CLIMBED, HUNG, RISKED HIS LIFE.` · then, large: `PAY TODAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay one bill or debt promptly. Settle, and breathe. Think of what you owe that's sitting on your list. Not just bills. The babysitter you meant to pay back. The friend who covered lunch. The contractor's invoice. The kid down the street who mowed the lawn. Picture the person on the other end, not the amount. What are they waiting to do with it? Choose one, and decide to pay it before today's sunset. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion where a worker's pay can't wait past sundown.
Your line: pay today. Before the sun goes down, pay one person you owe, especially someone who works for you. Day five hundred nine.

510.title: Ki Teitzei: the forgotten sheaf (Deuteronomy 24:19)
510.hook: a sheaf left behind by accident belongs to the poor
510.howItsDone: The laws of the forgotten sheaf, the corner of the field and gleanings are set out in the Mishnah's tractate Peah, and some farmers in the land of Israel still observe them; elsewhere they are studied as the root of Jewish giving to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the worker paid before sunset. Your line was pay today. Who did you pay? Today, still in the fields, a commandment you can only keep by accident. Day five hundred ten.

Harvest day, a long time ago. The reapers have been cutting grain since dawn, binding it into sheaves, stacking them on the cart. The light is going. Everyone's tired. The farmer takes one last look across the field, and there, at the far edge, is a sheaf someone missed. A whole bundle of grain, lying in the stubble. Every instinct says walk back and get it. It's yours. You grew it. And the Torah says: don't.
screen: `HARVEST, FROM DAWN TO DUSK.` → `ONE SHEAF MISSED.` → `DON'T GO BACK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou reapest thy harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go back to fetch it; it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow." The same goes for olives: don't beat the branches a second time. And grapes: don't go back over the vines. What's left belongs to the people who have no field. The Hebrew name for the forgotten sheaf is shichecha, from the word for forgetting. And here's the odd thing about it. Many commandments can be planned. You set aside, you measure, you decide. This one can only be kept by accident. If you leave a sheaf on purpose, it's a gift, a good one, but it isn't shichecha. Only what you truly forgot counts. The verse ends with a promise: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thy hands. Rashi, quoting the early midrash, notices how strange that is. You're blessed for something you didn't even mean to do? Yes, he says, and how much more for good you do on purpose. And then he draws a line to everyday life: if a coin falls out of your pocket and a poor person finds it and lives on it, you're blessed through it too. There's even a story in the Tosefta of a pious man who discovered he'd forgotten a sheaf, and was so happy at getting to fulfill this commandment that he told his son to bring offerings of thanks. A mistake, turned into a gift.
screen: `DON'T GO BACK FOR IT.` · `SHICHECHA: THE FORGOTTEN ONE.` · `KEPT ONLY BY ACCIDENT.` · `THE DROPPED COIN.` · then, large: `FORGOTTEN BECOMES GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one lost thing become a gift. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you lost or left behind lately and still feel a small sting about. The umbrella on the train. The twenty that slipped out of your pocket. The jacket at the restaurant. Instead of the sting, try the farmer's view. Someone may have found it, and needed it. Let it go as a gift you didn't know you were giving. Then think: is there anything you're keeping that you've really forgotten you own? The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion where a forgotten sheaf belongs to the stranger, the orphan and the widow.
Your line: forgotten becomes given. Today, when you lose or forget something small, don't chase it. Bless whoever finds it. Day five hundred ten.

511.title: Ki Teitzei: the stragglers (Deuteronomy 25:17–19)
511.hook: Amalek attacked the weary at the back of the line
511.howItsDone: Jews read Deuteronomy 25:17–19 aloud on Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath before Purim, and Jewish law treats hearing it read each year as a duty; it is also read at the close of Ki Teitzei in late summer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shichecha, the forgotten sheaf left for the poor. Your line was forgotten becomes given. Did you let something lost go as a gift? Today, the last words of Ki Teitzei, and a command to remember. Day five hundred eleven.

Watch a big group on the move and the line starts to stretch. A school trip, a hike, a crowd leaving a stadium. The fast walkers pull ahead. The middle keeps pace. And at the back, a gap opens: the kid with the blister, the grandmother who needs to rest, the dad carrying a toddler on his shoulders. Nobody decides to leave them behind. The line just gets longer. Deuteronomy remembers the day someone noticed that gap and used it.
screen: `A LINE STRETCHES.` → `THE GAP AT THE BACK.` → `SOMEONE USED IT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way as ye came forth out of Egypt; how he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were enfeebled in thy rear, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God." The story itself is in Exodus, a battle at a place called Rephidim, soon after the sea. Deuteronomy adds the detail that matters. Amalek didn't attack the army at the front. He went for the back of the line, the enfeebled, the faint, the weary. The ones who couldn't fight and couldn't run. And he feared not God: no line he wouldn't cross. The portion ends with a strange double command. Blot out the memory of Amalek, and, in the same breath: "thou shalt not forget." Erase the name, keep the lesson. The rabbis set this passage to be read on the Sabbath before Purim, called Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath of remembering, because tradition traces Haman, the villain of the Purim story, to Amalek. Some rabbinic authorities hold that the ancient nation of Amalek can no longer be identified, and some teachers read Amalek as a way of acting, preying on the weak, that can show up anywhere, even in us. So the memory has two edges. Remember what was done to the stragglers. And notice who's at the back of your own line, because whoever stands there is the one most easily left behind, and most easily hurt.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look after whoever is at the back. Settle, and breathe. Picture the lines you're part of. Your family, your team at work, your friend group, your congregation, your class. Who in each one is falling behind? The coworker who's quietly drowning. The cousin no one calls. The friend who stopped showing up. The kid who's slower at reading. Find one. You don't have to fix their life. Just picture walking back down the line to where they are, and keeping pace with them for a while. The bell holds the time.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. A portion crowded with commandments, ending with the weary at the back of the line.

Your line: watch the stragglers. A week of trees spared, the nearest town, the mother bird, the railing, wages paid by sunset, the forgotten sheaf, and now the back of the line. Today, reach out to one person who's falling behind. Day five hundred eleven.
